title: Announcing the First Long Now Labs Awardees
gist: Long Now and the Protocol Institute announce awardees of the first two Protocols for the Long Now Labs: three $25,000 Book of Time prototypes (including a Bitcoin-based thermodynamic clock for LLMs) and Nina Begus as lead of Epistemic Cycles, studying information ruptures.

insights.claim: Three Book of Time awardees each receive $25,000 plus support to build prototypes over the next year, with an anthology of 27 selected submissions to publish in spring 2027.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Shows funding scale and timeline of this long-term-thinking program.

insights.claim: Sarah Friend will test whether LLMs behave differently when they can verify time via Bitcoin's blockchain, a clock no single party controls because each block takes real energy to produce.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Novel use of proof-of-work as a trusted time source for AI; niche but links Bitcoin to AI-agent infrastructure.

insights.claim: LLMs are discontinuous clocks: they have dataset cutoffs and only know the date because it is injected into the context window, and stale conversations do not get time updates.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Time-awareness is a real limitation of deployed models and a design consideration for agents.
insights.quote: The only reason it knows it’s not still 02024 is because the date is injected into the context window.
insights.locator: What kind of clock is an LLM?

insights.claim: Matthew Caren and Anastasha Rachel Gunawan's Lagu Hantu is a gamelan-inspired instrument that answers players with recorded fragments of past performers making similar gestures, framing archives as rituals rather than repositories.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Cultural-art example; low direct investment relevance.

insights.claim: Eirini Malliaraki's One Billion Clocks will build a kinetic public sculpture making the nested metabolic timescales of living soil perceptible at human scale.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation

insights.claim: Nina Begus of UC Berkeley will lead Epistemic Cycles through 2027, producing an atlas and typology of historical information ruptures from writing and accounting to generative AI and how societies repaired them.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Source of frameworks on how societies respond to AI-driven truth disruption.
insights.locator: Epistemic Cycles sought an individual or team

insights.claim: Begus argues epistemic crises are rarely caused by a new medium alone but arise when a technology makes inherited methods and vocabularies inadequate to new challenges, rejecting technological determinism.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Implies institutional adaptation, not the technology itself, determines the severity of misinformation shocks.
insights.quote: Epistemic crises are rarely caused by a new medium alone, as technological determinism would have it

insights.claim: The Protocols for the Long Now open call in April 2026 drew 378 submissions across both Labs; a third Lab, Interspecies Protocols, launches in 2027.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Indicates demand and pipeline for the program.
